records.title: Successful Treatment of Onchocerca lupi Auricular Infestation Causing Severe Otitis Externa in a Dog.
records.abstract: We report the first successfully treated case of auricular Onchocerca lupi infection in a dog in Switzerland, causing severe unilateral otitis externa. Diagnosis was confirmed by molecular analysis after nematode extraction. Combined therapy led to complete remission within 6 weeks, highlighting O. lupi as a differential for chronic otitis with mass formation.

records.title: Sex steroids in animals absent gonads: A case series.
records.abstract: Identifying possible sources of sex steroids is challenging in animals exhibiting apparent responses in reproductive tissues but presenting with a history of having been neutered. Sex steroids, typically secreted by the gonads, also induce responses in non-reproductive tissues including the skin or brain, sometimes affecting behaviors. The analysis of hormones has become a mainstay of diagnostic endocrinology in small and large animal practice. The repertoire of those with reproductive relevance has expanded significantly with specific immunoassays detecting anti-Müllerian hormone (AMH) from either ovarian granulosa or testicular Sertoli cells. This has proven to be extremely useful differentiating neutered animals from those that are not. When AMH is undetectable, indicating neutered status, the possibility of sex steroid secretion by non-gonadal, pathological tissue, or other exogenous sources becomes very real. Reported gonadal status (as stated by owners) is not always reliable given that changes of ownership are common, and neutering is not always complete, complicating initial diagnosis. The cases reported here include several that are unique in either their presentation, diagnostic approach or likely etiologic origin. All were submitted primarily for an assessment of their gonadal status. Collectively, they illustrate, with unusual insight, the utility of AMH as a gonadal biomarker, while obviating the complexity of interpretation of reproductive hormone analyses in supposedly gonadectomized cats, horses and dogs manifesting a variety of apparent, reproductive conditions and pathologies.

records.title: Ecological Implications of Rodenticide Exposure: First Evidence of Bromadiolone Poisoning in an Indian Leopard ( Panthera pardus fusca ).
records.abstract: Large carnivores such as Indian leopard ( Panthera pardus fusca ) play a crucial role in maintaining ecosystem stability. However, they face increasing threats from habitat loss and other anthropogenic pressures. One significant but underreported threat is unintentional or deliberate poisoning, particularly from chemical pesticides. This study reports the first documented case of rodenticide (bromadiolone) poisoning in a large mammalian carnivore in India. In this study, a deceased female leopard (~5 years old) was recovered from the Nilgiris Forest Division, Tamil Nadu, India. Tissues of kidney, liver, and gut contents of the leopard were collected for toxicological investigation. Using high-performance liquid chromatography-mass spectrometry (LC-MS/MS), the samples were screened for 51 pesticides. Bromadiolone, a second-generation anticoagulant rodenticide (SGAR), was detected at concentrations of 802.9 ng/g in kidney, 237.7 ng/g in liver, and 39.3 ng/g in gut. No other pesticides were detected in any of the samples studied. Postmortem examination revealed internal hemorrhaging consistent with bromadiolone-induced coagulopathy, confirming it as the likely cause of death. This study underscores the ecological risk posed by rodenticides through deliberate or secondary poisoning of nontarget wildlife. To prevent such incidents, stricter regulations and greater public awareness regarding the use of anticoagulant rodenticides near forested areas are urgently needed. Additionally, long-term monitoring and research on rodenticide exposure are strongly recommended to guide further conservation actions and safeguard wildlife across the country.

records.title: Feline parasitic pneumonia caused by Troglostrongylus brevior: a case report.
records.journal: Revista brasileira de parasitologia veterinaria = Brazilian journal of veterinary parasitology : Orgao Oficial do Colegio Brasileiro de Parasitologia Veterinaria
records.abstract: Nematodes represent an important etiological factor in verminous bronchopneumonia in domestic cats. Traditionally, Aelurostrongylus abstrusus and Capillaria aerophila were considered the principal parasitic species colonizing feline respiratory tract. However, in recent years, the clinical relevance of Troglostrongylus brevior has been increasingly recognized. This report describes a feline case characterized by chronic cough and persistent rhinitis lasting for four months. Thoracic radiography and ultrasonography revealed pulmonary alterations consistent with pneumonia. Routine hematological and copromicroscopic examinations yielded no significant findings. Definitive diagnosis was achieved through bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL) sampling followed by duplex polymerase chain reaction (PCR), which confirmed parasitic pneumonia attributable to T. brevior. Therapeutic management consisted of a topical spot-on formulation containing imidacloprid 40 mg and moxidectin 4 mg, administered on days 1 and 28. Clinical reassessment was performed on days 28, 56, 84, 112, and 140 post-treatment initiation. By day 140, all clinical signs had resolved completely. Follow-up thoracic radiographs and lung ultrasonography demonstrated no pathological changes. To the authors' knowledge, this is the first case report describing confirmed feline troglostrongylosis in Lithuania. Future studies should further investigate the epidemiological significance of cats in T. brevior infection, including the prevalence and distribution of the parasite within feline populations.

records.title: Laparoscopic-assisted treatment of giant urachal cyst in a female Dachshund.
records.abstract: To describe the clinical features and successful surgical management of a giant, symptomatic urachal cyst (UC) in a dog using a laparoscopic-assisted approach without partial cystectomy. Case report. A 10-year-old, 4.6 kg, spayed female Dachshund. The dog presented with urinary incontinence, pollakiuria, and abdominal distension. Computed tomography (CT) and cystography identified a 13-cm cystic lesion at the bladder apex without luminal communication. A laparoscopic exploration was initially attempted either for cyst resection, or for decortication combined with omentalization. Following percutaneous aspiration of the cyst, the lesion was dissected from the surrounding omental adhesion. Due to the inability to identify the course of both ureters and the indistinct anatomical margins between the cyst and the bladder, the procedure was converted to a mini-laparotomy. The cystic wall was readily separated from the bladder apex by blunt dissection and completely excised after circumferential incision at the external junction between the cyst and the bladder using a vessel sealing device. Following omentalization of the cyst resection site, the bladder was returned to its anatomical position within the peritoneal cavity. Postoperative recovery was uneventful. Transient apical bulging and discomfort during bladder distension were observed on postoperative cystography, attributed to a localized compliance mismatch between the denuded bladder wall and the stiffer, thermally coagulated region. Bladder capacity normalized by day 21 with a normal bladder silhouette. Histopathology confirmed a subserosal UC with no evidence of malignancy. The patient remained clinically well, and no recurrence was noted during a 20-month follow-up. Laparoscopic-assisted resection was an effective, minimally invasive treatment for the giant UC in this dog. Consistent with current human medical guidelines, simple marginal excision without partial cystectomy proved feasible and sufficient for a UC lacking luminal communication, regardless of lesion size.

records.title: Squamous cell carcinoma involving the anal sac region in a cat: clinical course and multimodal management with toceranib and electrochemotherapy.
records.abstract: Squamous cell carcinoma (SCC) is one of the most common malignant epithelial tumours in cats, typically arising in the oral cavity or at cutaneous sites, whereas involvement of the anal sac region is exceptionally rare, with only two cases previously reported. An 8-year-old neutered male Domestic Shorthair cat was referred for persistent tenesmus, constipation and anorexia. A perianal swelling had initially been interpreted as anal sacculitis on cytology, but incisional biopsies confirmed SCC, characterised histologically by only moderate atypia and a low mitotic count. Contrast-enhanced computed tomography revealed a non-circumferential mass centred on the left anal sac region with infiltration of the perirectal soft tissues causing partial rectal obstruction, together with regional lymphadenomegaly; nodal metastasis was confirmed cytologically. Surgery and radiation therapy were declined, and palliative treatment with toceranib phosphate and meloxicam was started. After approximately one month of clinically stable disease, one session of electrochemotherapy with intravenous bleomycin was performed. Clinical signs transiently improved, but rapid progression occurred shortly thereafter, with invasion of the pelvic urethra. The cat died 68 days after diagnosis. Despite reassuring histological features, the tumour showed aggressive local behaviour and early regional metastasis. Toceranib was associated with transient clinical improvement and electrochemotherapy produced only short-lived improvement, likely because the lesion's extent and depth precluded complete treatment of the tumour volume. This case documents aggressive behaviour in an SCC involving the anal sac region and supports considering SCC in cats with persistent perianal swelling, tenesmus or defecatory difficulty unresponsive to medical treatment.

records.title: Genomic analysis of extended-spectrum β-lactamase-producing Escherichia coli and Klebsiella pneumoniae isolated from a dog with a severe episode of self-trauma and urinary tract infection.
records.abstract: Extended-spectrum β-lactamase (ESBL)-producing Enterobacterales are emerging pathogens of major importance in veterinary medicine. This study describes the clinical, microbiological, and genomic characteristics of ESBL-producing Escherichia coli and Klebsiella pneumoniae isolated from a dog with paraparesis and concurrent pyelonephritis, chronic cystitis, and a self-traumatized limb lesion. A 12-year-old mixed-breed female dog underwent repeated antimicrobial therapy during hospitalization. Urine obtained by cystocentesis and wound samples were cultured, and ESBL-producing strains were characterized by antimicrobial susceptibility testing and whole-genome sequence-based analysis. CTX-M-55-producing E. coli sequence type (ST) 457, phylogroup F, O11:H25, and fimH145, was recovered from urine and wound samples, while the wound sample also yielded a CTX-M-15- and SHV-2-producing K. pneumoniae ST39, KL149:OL2α.2. The two closely related E. coli strains differed by 96 single nucleotide polymorphisms, despite sharing the same ST, resistome, plasmid replicons, and virulence profile. ESBL-positive strains carried multiple virulence genes, with the E. coli strains classified as extraintestinal pathogenic E. coli strains. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first report of ESBL-producing K. pneumoniae ST39 in an animal in Brazil. The co-occurrence of ESBL-producing E. coli ST457 and K. pneumoniae ST39 in the same dog highlights the potential for companion animals to harbor clinically relevant multidrug-resistant lineages and reinforces the need for continuous antimicrobial resistance monitoring and antimicrobial stewardship in this sector.

records.title: Hypocalcemia Secondary to Inadvertent Denosumab (Prolia) Administration in a 4-Month-Old Cat.
records.journal: Journal of veterinary emergency and critical care (San Antonio, Tex. : 2001)
records.abstract: To describe the clinical presentation, diagnosis, and management of hypocalcemia secondary to inadvertent administration of denosumab in a 4-month-old kitten. A 4-month-old neutered female domestic shorthair kitten was presented with acute weakness, tremors, third eyelid prolapse, and ataxia for several hours. Physical examination revealed lethargy, tachycardia, hypothermia, mild dehydration, and apparent nausea. Neurologic findings included tremors, cerebellar ataxia, bilateral mydriasis, and decreased bilateral direct and indirect pupillary reflexes. ECG confirmed sinus tachycardia. Blood work showed severe ionized hypocalcemia (0.74 mmol/L [2.96 mg/dL]; reference interval [RI]: 1.10-1.40 [4.40-5.60]), mild hypokalemia (3.38 mmol/L [3.38 mEq/L]; RI: 3.90-4.90 [3.90-4.90]), and moderate hyperglycemia (10.8 mmol/L [194 mg/dL]; RI: 3.6-6.2 [64.86-111.71]). The owner later disclosed an accidental subcutaneous injection to the kitten with denosumab 1 week earlier, strongly suggesting drug-induced hypocalcemia. Treatment with IV calcium gluconate 10% (0.5 mL/kg over 10 min twice) resolved signs and normalized iCa (1.20 mmol/L [4.8 mg/dL]). Isotonic crystalloids with potassium and maropitant were given for hydration, electrolyte correction, and nausea. Oral calcium (60 mg/kg, q 24 h) was started on Day 1; iCa remained normal (1.26 mmol/L [5.04 mg/dL]) at Day 2, and the kitten was discharged. At Day 11, iCa was 1.19 mmol/L [4.76 mg/dL], the dose was halved, and at Day 18, iCa remained normal (1.24 mmol/L [4.96 mg/dL]), allowing for discontinuation of therapy. This report describes hypocalcemia secondary to inadvertent administration of denosumab to a kitten. The clinical manifestations and diagnosis are described, along with the details of management that led to the kitten in this report making a full recovery.

records.title: Ovarian leiomyoma with an epithelioid differentiation in a dog.
records.journal: The Journal of veterinary medical science
records.abstract: A 12-years-3-months-old female Toy Poodle underwent ovariohysterectomy, and an 8-mm ovarian mass was incidentally identified on pathological examination. On the cut surface, the mass consisted of a yellowish-white solid oval area surrounded by a soft white crescent-shaped peripheral area. Histopathologically, the oval area was composed of interlacing fascicles of spindle neoplastic cells with elongated to cigar-shaped nuclei, whereas the crescent-shaped peripheral area contained solitary or clustered polygonal to round neoplastic cells scattered within myxoid stroma. Immunohistochemically, both tumor cell populations were positive for α-smooth muscle actin, desmin, and vimentin. Cytokeratin expression was observed in the polygonal to round neoplastic cells, but not in the spindle neoplastic cells. Collectively, the tumor was diagnosed as an ovarian leiomyoma with an epithelioid differentiation.

records.title: Magnetic resonance imaging features and management of recurrent spinal inflammatory pseudotumor with intramedullary extension in a dog.
records.journal: The Journal of veterinary medical science
records.abstract: A 4-year-old intact female mixed-breed dog was admitted with a 2-month history of progressive thoracic and pelvic limb paresis. Neurological examination localized the lesion to the cervical spine. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) revealed a well-defined mass of the spinal cord extending from the third to fifth cervical vertebral level. The mass was T2-weighted hypointense, T1-weighted isointense, with homogeneous contrast enhancement. Based on the surgical, histopathological, and microbiologic findings, the lesion was diagnosed as an inflammatory pseudotumor. At 55 days postoperatively, the patient demonstrated marked gait improvement, and MRI confirmed successful mass removal with a small residual intramedullary lesion at the C5 level. Follow-up MRI at day 118 exhibited tumor recurrence, and hypofractionated radiotherapy was administered. One month after treatment, MRI demonstrated lesion size reduction.

records.title: Intraocular carcinosarcoma with osteosarcomatous component arising from iridociliary adenocarcinoma in a dog.
records.journal: The Journal of veterinary medical science
records.abstract: A 9-year-old neutered male Labrador Retriever presented with increased intraocular pressure in the left eye and underwent enucleation for a suspected intraocular tumor. Grossly, a white to greyish-white solid mass occupied the anterior segment and was partially contiguous with the lens. Histologically, the tumor exhibited biphasic proliferation of epithelial and mesenchymal components. The mesenchymal component showed osteoid formation, and transitional features were observed between the two components. Based on histological and immunohistochemical findings, the tumor was diagnosed as a carcinosarcoma composed of an iridociliary adenocarcinoma component and an osteosarcomatous component. This is the first report of carcinosarcoma in the canine eye, expanding the understanding of the morphological diversity and histogenetic characteristics of canine iridociliary tumors.

records.title: Histological and proteomic characterization of hyaline material in two dogs with hyalinizing pancreatic adenocarcinoma.
records.journal: The Journal of veterinary medical science
records.abstract: Hyalinizing pancreatic adenocarcinoma is a rare subtype of exocrine pancreatic carcinoma in dogs, characterized by abundant extracellular hyaline material within the tumor. In this study, we investigated two canine cases exhibiting this distinctive hyalinizing morphology using histological, proteomic, immunohistochemical, ultrastructural, and molecular approaches. Histological examination revealed amyloid-like eosinophilic hyaline deposits; however, these deposits lacked diagnostic features of amyloid, as confirmed by Congo red and thioflavin S staining and transmission electron microscopy. Liquid chromatography-tandem mass spectrometry (LC-MS/MS) identified bile salt-activated lipase (BAL) as the predominant component of the hyaline deposits. Immunohistochemistry confirmed strong anti-BAL immunoreactivity in the deposits. In addition to BAL, amyloid-associated proteins, including clusterin, vitronectin, apolipoprotein E, and apolipoprotein A-I, were detected. Together with the negative Congo red and thioflavin S staining and ultrastructural findings, these results support that the hyaline deposits are BAL-rich, non-amyloid extracellular deposits. Some deposits also contained collagen, indicating biochemical heterogeneity of the hyaline material. RT-qPCR analysis suggested higher CEL, and lower GRP94 expression in hyalinizing pancreatic adenocarcinomas than in non-hyalinizing pancreatic carcinomas. These observations raise a hypothesis that excessive BAL production, together with reduced GRP94-mediated chaperone support, may contribute to extracellular accumulation of aggregated BAL. Collectively, this study identifies BAL as the predominant component of hyaline deposits in canine hyalinizing pancreatic adenocarcinoma based on LC-MS/MS analysis and highlights a non-amyloid protein aggregation process associated with this tumor subtype.

records.title: A dog with suspected hypothalamic hypoadrenocorticism classified by corticotropin-releasing hormone (CRH) testing.
records.journal: The Journal of veterinary medical science
records.abstract: A 7-year-old intact male toy poodle presented with abdominal distension, polydipsia, and polyuria. Abdominal ultrasonography revealed bilateral adrenal atrophy, and adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH) stimulation testing showed persistently low cortisol concentrations with concurrent low endogenous ACTH, indicating central hypoadrenocorticism. To localize dysfunction within the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis, a corticotropin-releasing hormone (CRH) stimulation test was performed. Endogenous ACTH increased markedly after CRH administration, whereas cortisol remained undetectable, demonstrating preserved pituitary responsiveness and supporting a diagnosis of hypothalamic hypoadrenocorticism. Treatment of hypoadrenocorticism with prednisolone alone resulted in long-term clinical stabilization without electrolyte abnormalities for over one year. To our knowledge, this is the first canine report classifying suspected hypothalamic hypoadrenocorticism using CRH stimulation testing.

records.title: Esophageal strictures associated with prolonged nasoesophageal tube placement in three cats.
records.abstract: Nasoesophageal tube placement for a prolonged period of time has not previously been associated with esophageal stricture in cats. Three cats with suspected hepatic lipidosis required extended enteral nutritional support because voluntary food intake remained < 25% of the calculated resting energy requirement. The cumulative duration of nasoesophageal tube placement was 24-37 days. Regurgitation or retching developed within 1-3 days after tube removal, and esophagoscopy identified severe focal strictures in the cervical esophagus at the C4-C6 vertebral level in all 3 cats. One cat underwent 3 endoscopic balloon dilatation sessions at 1-week intervals, with enlargement of the esophageal lumen. The consistent anatomic location and temporal association with prolonged tube placement suggest that extended nasoesophageal intubation may be a risk factor for cervical esophageal stricture formation in cats. When prolonged nutritional support is anticipated, transition to a feeding tube intended for long-term use should be considered.

records.title: Acute Levothyroxine Overdose Followed by Serial Monitoring of Total Thyroxine and Thyroid-Stimulating Hormone in a Hypothyroid Dog.
records.abstract: Reports of acute levothyroxine overdose in dogs are rare with limited monitoring data. An 8-year-old spayed female Pomeranian receiving long-term hypothyroidism treatment presented 9 h after ingesting a one-month supply of levothyroxine (3 mg; 1.13 mg/kg). Except for transient tachycardia, the physical examination revealed unremarkable findings. The total thyroxine (T4) level exceeded the upper limit of quantification. Levothyroxine was discontinued, and activated charcoal and intravenous fluid were administered. The dog showed normal vital signs and no further clinical abnormalities during the 5-day hospitalisation. The total T4 concentration decreased and normalised by 73 h after the overdose. The canine thyroid-stimulating hormone (cTSH) concentrations were initially normal but exceeded the upper reference limit at 98 h. The patient was discharged on Day 5. Two days later, levothyroxine was resumed because the dog exhibited signs of recurrent hypothyroidism with persistently elevated cTSH levels. Hypothyroidism was well-controlled for 6 months. To our knowledge, this is the first report to document a levothyroxine overdose in a hypothyroid dog using daily total T4 and cTSH monitoring. These findings suggest that acute overdose is less severe than chronic levothyroxine exposure.

records.title: Chronic Recurrent Septic Peritonitis in a Diabetic Dog Caused by Staphylococcus pseudintermedius With Splendore-Hoeppli Reaction (Botryomycosis-Like/Bacterial Pseudomycetoma).
records.abstract: A 6-year-old neutered male Miniature Pinscher with poorly regulated diabetes mellitus was evaluated for recurrent abdominal effusion, lethargy and inappetence secondary to chronic septic peritonitis. Across four discrete clinical episodes, Staphylococcus pseudintermedius was repeatedly isolated in pure culture from peritoneal fluid and omental tissue, with consistent antimicrobial susceptibility profiles across submissions, a pattern suggestive of strain persistence rather than serial reinfection. Histopathology of omental biopsies demonstrated severe, chronic pyogranulomatous peritonitis with prominent Splendore-Hoeppli material surrounding bacterial colonies, consistent with bacterial pseudomycetoma. Despite two exploratory laparotomies with extensive abdominal lavage, closed-suction peritoneal drainage, broad-spectrum systemic antimicrobial therapy, and a subsequent salvage protocol of combined intravenous and intraperitoneal meropenem administered via an ultrasound-guided peritoneal catheter, infection ultimately recurred and the dog was humanely euthanized. The case is consistent with biofilm-associated chronic infection compounded by immune-complex deposition and concurrent endocrine disease, and supports consideration of regional antimicrobial delivery as a salvage strategy in refractory septic peritonitis when source control and systemic therapy alone prove insufficient.

records.title: Chemodectoma Arising From the Abdominal Aorta in a 9-Year-Old Female Dog: Clinical, Histopathological and Immunohistochemstric Study.
records.abstract: Chemodectomas are uncommon, typically benign neoplasms derived from paraganglionic chemoreceptor tissues, most frequently arising in the heart base or carotid bodies of brachycephalic dogs. This report documents a detailed pathological description of a chemodectoma originating from the abdominal aorta in a non-human species, representing, to our knowledge, the first case specifically characterized by its origin at the aortic trifurcation, thereby expanding the recognized anatomical spectrum of this tumour entity. A 9-year-old spayed female terrier was presented with persistent panting, recent-onset obesity following previous cachexia, and a complex clinical history including polyuria/polydipsia and pyoderma. Haematological and biochemical analyses revealed a regenerative anaemia, leucocytosis, and biochemical indicators suggestive of cholestasis and potential endocrinopathy. Advanced imaging identified a solitary, well-demarcated, highly vascular abdominal mass closely associated with the aortic trifurcation. Given the tumour's inaccessibility and pronounced vascularity, cytological confirmation via fine needle aspiration was precluded due to haemorrhagic risk, necessitating exploratory laparotomy. Intraoperatively, the mass was unresectable because of its anatomical relationships and the prohibitive risk of catastrophic haemorrhage. Humane euthanasia was subsequently elected. Histopathological evaluation demonstrated a lobulated neoplasm composed of pleomorphic neuroendocrine cells, with low mitotic activity and an absence of necrosis or haemorrhage. Immunohistochemistry confirmed strong, diffuse synaptophysin reactivity and focal neuron-specific enolase positivity, while chromogranin A and S100 protein were negative, underscoring immunophenotypic variability. This case illustrates the diagnostic complexity and therapeutic limitations posed by extra-cardiac chemodectomas in veterinary species, especially when located in unconventional anatomical sites. Limitations included the unavailability of computed tomography and lack of postoperative follow-up. This report expands the recognized clinico-pathological spectrum of chemodectomas and highlights the necessity for multidisciplinary diagnostic strategies and further research aimed at defining optimal management protocols for such rare and challenging presentations.

records.title: Primary Erythrocytosis (Polycythaemia) in a Neutered Male Dog Presenting With Right Hindlimb Lameness.
records.abstract: A 2-year-old male entire Cocker Spaniel was referred for investigation of progressive right hindlimb lameness and polyuria and polydipsia. Investigations conducted by the primary care veterinary surgeon revealed erythrocytosis (haematocrit of 78%, reference interval: 37%-55%) and urine concentration consistent with polyuria and polydipsia (specific gravity 1.014). Upon referral, physical examination revealed a dark red oral mucosa and right hindlimb lameness, characterised by intermittent non-weight bearing of the limb when standing. Neurological examination only revealed a mild short-strided gait, and orthopaedic examination was unremarkable. Secondary causes of erythrocytosis were excluded by normal arterial blood gas, low erythropoietin levels and normal thoracic and abdominal imaging, resulting in a diagnosis of primary erythrocytosis (PE). Focal ultrasonography identified a right external iliac venous thrombus, suspected to be the cause of the right hindlimb lameness and presumed to be associated with the PE. Initial management involved repeated phlebotomies, followed by long-term treatment with hydroxyurea (31 mg/kg twice weekly) and rivaroxaban (2 mg/kg once daily). At the 5-month recheck, the dog was asymptomatic, with resolution of the iliac thrombus and a normal haematocrit. This case highlights an unusual presentation of PE in a dog, not previously described in the veterinary literature, and re-examines the discussion on the optimal management of this rare condition, with a focus on the necessity of antithrombotic therapy.

records.title: Unilateral Hormonally Active Testicular Sertoli Cell Tumour and Feminization Syndrome in a Bernese Mountain Dog With Normally Descended Testes.
records.abstract: To describe the clinical presentation, diagnostic workup and successful outcome of a hormonally active testicular Sertoli cell tumour (SCT) in a non-cryptorchid Bernese Mountain Dog. A 10-year-old intact male dog was evaluated with a history of progressive alopecia, gynaecomastia and haematuria. Diagnostic investigations included complete blood count, serum biochemistry, oestradiol assay, abdominal and testicular ultrasonography, preputial cytology and histopathological examination following bilateral orchiectomy. Clinical signs included bilaterally symmetrical alopecia, hyperpigmentation and a pendulous prepuce. Laboratory findings revealed mild non-regenerative anaemia and severe hyperestrogenism (oestradiol: 119 pg/mL). Preputial cytology showed a predominance of superficial epithelial cells (> 80%), supporting the state of hyperestrogenism. Ultrasonography identified a large, vascularized left testicular mass and cystic prostatic changes. Histopathology confirmed an SCT. Following surgery, clinical signs and laboratory abnormalities resolved completely within 9 months. This case emphasizes that SCTs should be a differential diagnosis for feminization syndrome in older dogs even without cryptorchidism. It also highlights preputial cytology as a rapid and effective minimally invasive tool for the preliminary identification of hyperestrogenism.

records.title: Intraoperative Indocyanine Green Fluorescence for Assessment of Suspected Venous Invasion in a Dog With Thyroid Carcinoma.
records.abstract: Accurate intraoperative assessment of vascular involvement in canine thyroid carcinoma remains challenging when preoperative imaging findings are equivocal. This case describes the use of intraoperative indocyanine green fluorescence imaging to assist real-time assessment of suspected venous involvement during canine thyroidectomy. A 5-year-old spayed female Maltese dog was presented with a cervical mass and clinicopathological findings consistent with hypothyroidism. Contrast-enhanced computed tomography identified a left thyroid mass with suspected external jugular vein compression but no definitive evidence of vascular invasion. records.title: Carotid body carcinoma in a French bulldog treated with toceranib phosphate.

records.title: Clinical and  18 F-FDG PET/CT imaging features in a dog with bacterial sepsis of unknown origin.
records.journal: The Canadian veterinary journal = La revue veterinaire canadienne
records.abstract: Positron emission tomography with 2-deoxy-2-[fluorine-18] fluoro-D-glucose integrated with computed tomography ( 18 F-FDG PET/CT) imaging identified infection and inflammation earlier and with higher sensitivity than other imaging modalities in human medicine. A small case series explored the use of  18 F-FDG PET/CT for detecting the cause of fever of unknown origin in dogs. The  18 F-FDG PET/CT revealed moderate, patchy FDG avidity and soft-tissue swelling of the left carpus and tarsus (SUV max: 7.18 and SUV max: 5.58, respectively), moderate heterogeneous splenic and hepatic hypermetabolic activity (SUV max: 3.42), and bilaterally symmetric renal hypermetabolic activity (SUV max: 6.22) without appropriate flourine-18 fluorodeoxyglucose ( 18 F-FDG) excretion. Other notable findings included marked, diffuse  18 F-FDG uptake within all bone marrow spaces (SUV max: 15.47) and a generalized, mild lymphadenopathy with moderate hypermetabolic activity. Positive blood cultures confirmed sepsis. Clinical deterioration despite appropriate antibiotic and supportive therapy prompted euthanasia. Necropsy revealed lymphohistiocytic and neutrophilic necrotizing vasculitis with thrombosis and necrosis in heart, spleen, brain, and liver, consistent with septicemia.  Enterococcus faecium  was isolated from lungs, kidneys, and spleen;  Serratia marcescens  was isolated from lungs and kidneys. This is the first documented report of the use of  18 F-FDG PET/CT for the diagnostic workup of a septic patient in veterinary medicine with corroborative necropsy findings to confirm PET/CT suspicion of disseminated septicemia. Key clinical message: Positron emission tomography with 2-deoxy-2-[fluorine-18] fluoro-D-glucose integrated with computed tomography imaging, which combines the functional, metabolic information from a PET scan with the high-resolution anatomical detail from a CT scan, should be considered as an adjunctive imaging modality for the diagnostic workup to identify focal and systemic infections in veterinary medicine. records.title: Ultrasonographic features and clinical outcome of an anaplastic carcinoma arising from a uterus masculinus in an intact, non-cryptorchid male dog.

records.abstract: A 6-year-old intact male dog was referred because of persistent hematuria despite multiple courses of antimicrobial therapy. Exploratory laparotomy confirmed the presence of a uterus masculinus with blind-ended uterine horns, associated adhesions, and a large mass arising from the right cranial aspect. Surgical excision of the abnormal structure and orchiectomy were carried out. Histopathology confirmed an anaplastic carcinoma of Müllerian origin arising from persistent Müllerian duct remnants. There was rapid clinical deterioration after surgery, including imaging findings consistent with pulmonary, hepatic, and peritoneal metastatic disease, ultimately leading to euthanasia 5 wk after diagnosis. records.title: Treatment of Refractory Vomiting With Traditional Chinese Veterinary Medicine in Two Dogs and a Cat: A Cases Series.
records.abstract: Refractory vomiting in dogs and cats is a common clinical condition in small animal practice, typically characterized by recurrent vomiting, belching and related symptoms, which is a great challenge to veterinarians. According to Traditional Chinese Veterinary Medicine (TCVM), this condition is primarily attributed to dysfunction of the spleen and stomach in transformation and transportation, leading to the upward rebellion of stomach Qi. Derived from the Shang Han Lun (Treatise on Cold Damage), Xuanfu Daizhe Decoction functions to direct rebellious Qi downward, resolve phlegm, tonify Qi and harmonize the stomach. It is mainly indicated for conditions resulting from stomach Qi counter flow. In this report, three cases of refractory vomiting in two dogs and a cat diagnosed as stomach Qi rebellion according to TCVM were treated with modified Xuanfu Daizhe Decoction based on syndrome differentiation. The results showed that all three cases achieved favourable therapeutic outcomes. These findings suggest that, for refractory vomiting caused by stomach Qi rebellion in dogs and cats, individualized treatment with modified Xuanfu Daizhe Decoction based on specific clinical presentations can achieve stable and reliable efficacy.

records.title: Novel Therapy for Severe Bilateral Pyogranulomatous Blepharitis Secondary to Hyaluronic Acid Filler in a Dog.
records.abstract: A 9-year-old female spayed mixed breed dog was initially examined for severe bilateral entropion secondary to enophthalmos from chronic oral steroid use for immune-mediated thrombocytopenia as well as potential historic masticatory muscle myositis. records.title: Removal of a lodged endotracheal tube in an anaesthetised French Bulldog using manual laryngeal stabilisation and neuromuscular blockade, and subsequent complications.
records.abstract: A 5-year-old, female neutered French Bulldog presented under anaesthesia with an endotracheal tube (ETT) lodged in the larynx. The ETT was successfully removed under neuromuscular blockade with manual laryngeal stabilisation: the left thumb pressed against the epiglottis intraorally and the left index and middle fingers gripped the larynx externally to immobilise the larynx. The dog presented in respiratory distress 4 weeks later with tracheal stenosis that was successfully treated with tracheal resection and anastomosis. This case report describes the use of neuromuscular blockade and manual laryngeal stabilisation to remove a lodged ETT and reflects on the subsequent complications.

records.title: Rare Feline Gingival Extramedullary Plasmacytoma: Clinical Application of Electrochemotherapy for Local Control.
records.abstract: Feline extramedullary plasmacytoma (EMP) is an uncommon plasma cell neoplasm typically regarded as biologically benign; however, its clinical behaviour may be heterogeneous. This case report describes an aggressive gingival EMP in a 14-year-old neutered male Turkish Angora cat, characterised by alveolar bone lysis and cytologically confirmed regional lymph node metastasis in the absence of systemic features consistent with multiple myeloma. Histopathological examination revealed an infiltrative round cell neoplasm with high mitotic index, and strong diffuse MUM-1 immunoreactivity confirmed the diagnosis. As complete surgical excision was declined, and tumour regrowth occurred after repeated radiation therapy, electrochemotherapy (ECT) was selected for local tumour control. Bleomycin (15,000 IU/m 2  IV) was administered before pulse delivery, and three ECT sessions were performed at weekly intervals. The tumour volume decreased by more than 70%, which was consistent with a partial response, and only mild self-limiting local adverse effects were observed. No systemic toxicity was observed. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first report describing the use of ECT for feline gingival EMP. This case highlights the potential biological heterogeneity of feline EMP and suggests that ECT may provide short-term local tumour reduction and palliation when complete surgical excision is not feasible.

records.title: Spontaneous Reduction in Mitral Valve Regurgitation in Three Dogs With Severe Myxomatous Mitral Valve Disease: An Unusual Case Report.
records.abstract: Myxomatous mitral valve disease (MMVD), the most common heart disease in small-breed dogs, is characterized by mitral regurgitation (MR) resulting from valvular degeneration, which may progress to left-sided heart failure. This report describes the cases of three dogs with severe MMVD (American College of Veterinary Internal Medicine Stages C or D) who exhibited an unexpected spontaneous reduction in MR despite continued valve degeneration. Three dogs initially presented with symptoms of heart failure and left atrial and ventricular enlargement. Standard treatment, including diuretics, improved their conditions; however, further monitoring revealed that the coaptation gap decreased due to mitral valve thickening, leading to a reduction in MR. This was accompanied by a significant decrease in heart size. As a result, diuretics were discontinued, and all dogs were successfully managed with pimobendan alone. To our knowledge, this is the first report of spontaneous MR reduction in MMVD, where coaptation gap narrowing played a role in clinical improvement. These cases may broaden the current understanding of MMVD progression, suggesting that, in rare instances, changes in cardiac remodelling and clinical status can occur. Further research is warranted to better understand the underlying mechanisms.

records.title: Left Medial Liver Lobe Torsion Associated With Hepatocellular Carcinoma in a Pembroke Welsh Corgi: A Case Report.
records.abstract: Liver lobe torsion (LLT) is a rare, potentially life-threatening condition in dogs and is reported most often in medium- to large-breed dogs. Laboratory abnormalities included increased alanine aminotransferase and aspartate aminotransferase activities and C-reactive protein concentration. Computed tomography (CT) identified a 7.2 × 6.7 × 6.5 cm mass arising from the left medial liver lobe, a whirl sign at the base of the mass and a non-enhancing hypoattenuating region consistent with necrosis. Midline celiotomy and left medial liver lobectomy were performed without detorsion. Cytology of abdominal effusion was consistent with a culture-negative inflammatory exudate. Histopathology confirmed HCC with extensive necrosis, and the examined surgical margin was free of neoplastic cells. The dog recovered uneventfully, was discharged on postoperative Day 4 and had no recurrence of clinical abnormalities at 1-year follow-up. This case highlights the apparent association between HCC and LLT and the unusual location of the torsion axis at the base of the mass rather than at the hepatic hilus, although causality cannot be established from a single case. CT visualisation of the whirl sign at this atypical site was instrumental in establishing the preoperative diagnosis and guiding surgical planning.

records.title: Bilateral Keratouveitis and Secondary Glaucoma in a Young Dog With Immune-Mediated Polyarthritis and Systemic Inflammatory Response Syndrome.
records.abstract: A 7-month-old intact female mixed-breed dog presented emergently for inability to walk, lethargy, and vomiting. records.title: Anterior Segment OCT Diagnosis of Descemet's Membrane Detachment in a Cat With Suspected FIP-Associated Uveitis.
records.abstract: Persistent corneal edema in cats with anterior uveitis is often attributed to endothelial dysfunction; however, the underlying structural cause may not be apparent without advanced imaging. Descemet's membrane detachment (DMD) is rarely reported in cats and has not been well described in suspected feline infectious peritonitis (FIP)-associated uveitis. A 4-month-old intact male Norwegian Forest cat presented with severe unilateral granulomatous uveitis, mutton-fat keratic precipitates, diffuse stromal edema, and a 2+ aqueous flare. Aqueous humor PCR detected feline coronavirus RNA, although biotype testing did not confirm a mutation consistent with that associated with feline infectious peritonitis virus. As ocular inflammation progressed despite anti-inflammatory treatment, the nucleoside analog GS-441524 was administered along with anti-inflammatory and supportive ophthalmic treatment. Intraocular inflammation improved, but corneal edema persisted, prompting anterior segment optical coherence tomography (AS-OCT), which revealed planar DMD. Serial AS-OCT monitored posterior corneal structural changes. Corneal edema gradually decreased, and Descemet's membrane reapposition was documented by AS-OCT approximately one year after the initial presentation. Corneal clarity and stability were maintained without clinically evident recurrence for 18 months after reapposition was confirmed. This case describes the AS-OCT diagnosis and serial documentation of DMD and subsequent Descemet's membrane reapposition in a cat with suspected FIP-associated uveitis. These findings highlight the value of AS-OCT for identifying and monitoring posterior corneal abnormalities, including DMD, in cats with severe anterior uveitis and persistent corneal edema. The relationships among suspected FIP-associated uveitis, treatment, and DMD could not be determined from this single case.

records.abstract: To describe cases of canine idiopathic periocular granulomatous inflammation. Clinical records were reviewed. records.title: Staged caval occlusion enabling en bloc right divisional hepatectomy in two dogs with hepatocellular carcinoma.
records.abstract: To describe staged pre-renal caudal vena cava (CVC) occlusion before en bloc right divisional hepatectomy with segmental caval resection in two dogs with right divisional hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) involving the CVC. Gradual outpatient occlusion was performed over 79 and 44 days while monitoring saphenous venous pressure, renal values, and hindlimb edema. Macroscopically complete resection was achieved in both dogs. Complete HCC resection was confirmed histopathologically. In dog 2, no clinical signs suggestive of recurrence or metastasis were reported. Survival after hepatectomy was 352 and 2467 days. records.title: Bilateral Third Eyelid Ectopic Cilia in a Maine Coon Cat.
records.abstract: To describe a case of a Maine Coon cat diagnosed with bilateral aberrant hairs consistent with ectopic cilia arising from the third eyelid. The history, clinical signs, examination findings, surgical procedures, and case outcome were reviewed. Examination revealed a bilateral ocular discharge and follicular conjunctivitis; macroblepharon, permanent lower eyelid entropion associated with trichiasis, and non-ulcerative keratitis were present in the right eye. Surgical excision was curative, with no recurrence of epiphora, conjunctivitis, or the entropion.

records.title: Corneal Sequestration and Bilateral Distichiasis in a Binturong (Arctictis binturong).
records.abstract: To report the first documented case of corneal sequestration and distichiasis in a binturong (Arctictis binturong), discuss implications of disease prevalence in a non-domestic feliform, and hypothesize on potential etiology and predisposing factors for corneal sequestration. A 15-year-old intact male binturong. Anesthetized physical examination and ophthalmic assessment were performed by board-certified specialists. Corneal cytology, culture and sensitivity, debridement of the sequestra in lieu of keratectomy, histopathology, and cryoepilation were performed, followed by 4 weeks of topical therapy. The patient was euthanized 3 years later for unrelated reasons, and a necropsy was performed. Examination found bilateral distichiasis. In the left cornea, two brown, ovoid lesions flanked an area of yellow infiltrate, all overlying a raised, ulcerated granulation bed. Corneal cytology identified neutrophils, cocci, and rare rods. Histopathology of the debrided tissue showed coagulative to lytic necrosis with intralesional gram-positive cocci, indicating sequestration and secondary infection. Aerobic culture yielded Staphylococcus delphini and Streptococcus acidominimus. Photo updates 4 weeks post-operation showed resolution of clinical signs. Later, necropsy and histology showed chronic ocular changes without recurrence of sequestra. Clinical and histopathologic findings identified corneal sequestration, with chronic irritation secondary to distichiasis as a suspected factor. records.title: Characterization of  Escherichia marmotae , a novel pathogen causing urinary tract infection in a dog.
records.journal: Journal of veterinary diagnostic investigation : official publication of the American Association of Veterinary Laboratory Diagnosticians, Inc
records.abstract: Escherichia  is one of the most studied bacterial genera and includes several clinically significant pathogenic species. Unique strategies have evolved in members of this genus to allow their survival within different niches. Although initially the  Escherichia  cryptic clades (CCs) I-VIII were identified as environmental bacteria, they have been found as commensals and opportunistic pathogens in animals and humans. Notably, members of the  Escherichia  CCs are commonly mistaken for  E. coli  when using standard microbiologic techniques for species identification. We used whole-genome sequencing to correctly identify  E. marmotae -a member of the  Escherichia  CCs-that was initially misidentified as  E. coli  as the causative agent of a urinary tract infection (UTI) in a female dog. As a relatively new species that is phenotypically very similar to  E. coli , it is quite possible that  E. marmotae  infections may be underreported or misidentified. We hope that our work alerts veterinarians to consider  E. marmotae  as a possible cause of UTIs in dogs, especially because this could affect treatment decisions. Additionally, our findings broaden the current understanding of the  E. marmotae  ecology and host range.

records.abstract: A 3-month-old male Bernese Mountain dog was presented with a 10-day history of vomiting, vocalisation and abdominal discomfort following vaccination. records.abstract: Sporotrichosis caused by Sporothrix brasiliensis is an emerging zoonosis in South America, with Brazil representing the epicenter of a major ongoing epizootic. Antifungal susceptibility testing was performed to determine the minimum inhibitory concentration (MIC) of itraconazole. Both isolates were identified as S. brasiliensis and showed an itraconazole MIC of 0.03 mg/L. Both cats were successfully treated with oral itraconazole, achieving clinical cure after approximately five months of therapy. Zoonotic transmission to the owner occurred in both cases, confirming the public health implications of feline sporotrichosis. These cases document the first recognized feline and zoonotic outbreak caused by S. brasiliensis in Buenos Aires City and provide evidence of cat-to-cat and cat-to-human transmission. records.abstract: Peritoneal dialysis (PD)-associated peritonitis caused by zoonotic pathogens is uncommon and diagnostically challenging. records.title: First molecular characterization of Echinococcus granulosus sensu stricto genotype G1 from a common chimpanzee (Pan troglodytes) in the Kuwait Zoo.
records.abstract: Cystic echinococcosis (CE) is a cosmopolitan parasitic zoonosis with public health and economic significance. The content of the cyst was examined microscopically as well as by sequencing of the mitochondrial nad1 gene from one of the clonal protoscoleces found in the cyst. records.title: Primary Ciliary Dyskinesia with Secondary  Pseudomonas aeruginosa  Infection in a Dog: Endoscopic and Diagnostic Findings.
records.abstract: A 7-month-old, 3.6-kg, intact male Dachshund was presented with a lifelong history of chronic respiratory signs. records.title: Pulmonary Neoplasms with Pleuropulmonary Blastoma-like Features in Two Young Labrador Retrievers: Clinicopathological, Molecular and Comparative Characterisation.
records.abstract: Pleuropulmonary blastoma (PPB) is a rare, paediatric, mesenchymal, pulmonary neoplasm that can be highly aggressive. To date, there are only two reports of PPB in animals. We describe the finding of pulmonary neoplasms with PPB-like features in two unrelated Labrador Retrievers. Both dogs presented with acute dyspnoea, pneumothorax and pulmonary lesions. Treatment consisted of emergency thoracostomy tube placement followed by lung lobectomy. At follow-up, one dog experienced no recurrence 20 months post-surgery, whereas recurrence developed in the second dog 2 years postoperatively. Histopathological examination revealed spindle-shaped neoplastic cells with blastematous-to-sarcomatous appearance, associated with cystic spaces lined by non-neoplastic respiratory epithelium. Immunohistochemistry showed that the neoplastic cells were positive for mesenchymal markers but negative for epithelial and neuroendocrine markers, with some tumour cells showing desmin positivity, supportive of myogenic differentiation, possibly compatible with rhabdomyoblastic differentiation. Genome profiling revealed a heterogeneous somatic landscape. No pathogenic somatic or germline  DICER1  variants were found. We compared these findings with those reported in human PPB. This is the first comprehensive analysis of pulmonary neoplasms with PPB-like features in animals, and reveals parallels with PPB in humans, further supporting the 'One Medicine' approach.

records.title: Perioperative Glycemic Changes Following Partial Pancreatectomy for a Pancreatic Islet Cell Neoplasm in a Dog: A Case Report.
records.abstract: Canine insulinomas are functional pancreatic neuroendocrine tumors that typically cause hypoglycemia, but blood glucose may fluctuate before surgery and increase after resection. This report describes the diagnostic evaluation, surgical treatment, and perioperative glycemic course of a 12-year-old female Miniature Schnauzer with a pancreatic islet cell neoplasm considered clinically consistent with insulinoma. Intermittent low or low-normal blood glucose concentrations ranging from 54 to 72 mg/dL were documented before surgery, and the blood glucose concentration on the day of surgery was 73 mg/dL. Contrast-enhanced computed tomography identified a mass in the left pancreatic limb, and partial pancreatectomy was subsequently performed. Blood glucose reached 416 mg/dL 2 h after pancreatic mass removal while surgery was ongoing, then initially declined without insulin administration. Recurrent postoperative hyperglycemia was treated with regular insulin on postoperative days (PODs) 2 and 3, whereas subsequent decreases in blood glucose were treated with dextrose supplementation. Blood glucose continued to fluctuate on POD 4; no additional insulin was administered after POD 3. Histopathologic examination identified a pancreatic islet cell neoplasm. Although a paired serum insulin concentration during documented hypoglycemia was not available and immunohistochemical staining for insulin or other neuroendocrine markers was not performed, the clinical, imaging, glycemic, and histopathological findings were considered consistent with a clinicopathologic diagnosis of insulinoma. Blood glucose was 150 mg/dL on POD 7; subsequent recorded concentrations through POD 150 ranged from 107 to 133 mg/dL. Serial glucose monitoring helped characterize the perioperative course and guide postoperative insulin and dextrose treatment.

records.title: Case Report:  18 F-FDG PET/CT findings and SUVmax characterization in a dog with apocrine gland anal sac adenocarcinoma.
records.abstract: Apocrine gland anal sac adenocarcinoma (AGASACA) is a malignant epithelial tumor in dogs that commonly metastasizes to regional lymph nodes. Although  18 F-fluorodeoxyglucose ( 18 F-FDG) positron emission tomography/computed tomography (PET/CT) has been mentioned as a staging modality for this tumor, detailed imaging findings and maximum standardized uptake values (SUVmax) have not previously been reported. A 10-year-old castrated male Maltese was referred for a right anal sac mass and suspected lymph node metastasis. Preoperative  18 F-FDG PET/CT revealed increased uptake in the primary mass (SUVmax 7.3), the internal iliac lymph node (SUVmax 6.35), and the lumbar aortic lymph node (SUVmax 4.3), with no evidence of distant metastasis. Therefore, the dog was therefore classified as Stage IIIa. Based on these findings, intra-abdominal lymphadenectomy and right anal sacculectomy were performed. Histopathology confirmed AGASACA in the primary mass and morphologically similar metastatic adenocarcinoma in the resected lymph nodes. To our knowledge, this is the first report of  18 F-FDG PET/CT findings and SUVmax values in a dog with AGASACA and histologically confirmed lymph node metastases. These findings suggest that PET/CT may provide complementary metabolic information for preoperative nodal staging.

records.title: Cytologically Suggested Vulvar Involvement in a Dog with Multicentric Lymphoma After a Nodal Response to CHOP-Based Chemotherapy, with Discordant Clonality Results: A Case Report.
records.abstract: Involvement of the female reproductive tract is rare in canine lymphoma. A 9-year-old spayed female Maltese dog was presented with generalized lymphadenopathy. Splenectomy confirmed splenic large cell lymphoma, classified as World Health Organization clinical stage IVa. After 12 cycles of a CHOP (cyclophosphamide, doxorubicin, vincristine, and prednisolone)-based protocol, restaging computed tomography showed a marked reduction in all measurable lymph nodes, whereas gastric and subcutaneous nodules persisted. Disease progression was diagnosed by inguinal lymph node cytology, and rescue chemotherapy was started; however, the dog developed acute dyspnea and died two days later. records.title: A Salivary Conglomerate with a Substantial Organic Component Mimicking a Mineral Sialolith in the Mandibular-Sublingual Gland Complex of a Dog.
records.abstract: Solid lesions of the mandibular-sublingual salivary gland complex are rare in dogs. We report the case of an 11-year-old, 5 kg, intact female Maltese dog that presented with a non-painful, 2-3 cm left cervical swelling, soft at the surface and firm in depth. Fine-needle aspiration yielded clear, sero-mucous fluid. Radiographs revealed a well-defined, ovoid radiopaque structure measuring 3.1 × 2.9 cm in the cranial cervical region. Mandibular and monostomatic sublingual sialoadenectomy via a ventral approach revealed a large, heart-shaped, solid conglomerate within the glandular complex. Histopathological examination confirmed glandular atrophy, fibrosis and sialoadenitis. Fourier-transform infrared (FTIR) spectrometry of the submitted fragments indicated a substantial organic, protein- and lipid-rich component, with additional bands suggesting a possible minor mineral component. The dog healed completely, with no recurrence detected at the 2-week examination. Limitations include the absence of cross-sectional imaging and elemental analysis and the limited clinical follow-up. This case shows that protein-rich solid conglomerates should be included in the differential diagnosis of cervical swellings in dogs, that radiopacity alone does not establish mineral composition, and that complete surgical excision was associated with a favourable short-term outcome.

records.title: Multimodal Postmortem Investigation of Fatal Thoracic Metallic Projectile Trauma in a Jindo Dog: Radiographic, Computed Tomographic, Necropsy, and Histopathological Findings.
records.journal: Animals : an open access journal from MDPI
records.abstract: Metallic projectile injuries in companion animals present complex diagnostic and evidentiary challenges, especially when comprehensive crime scene data and intact projectiles are absent. This report describes the forensic postmortem investigation of an adult male Jindo dog submitted by law enforcement authorities following fatal penetrating trauma in South Korea. Digital radiography identified multiple radiopaque metallic opacities in the left thoracic region, accompanied by severe pleural effusion and subcutaneous emphysema. Postmortem computed tomography (PMCT; 16-slice MDCT, 0.75-mm slice thickness) precisely delineated clustered hyperattenuating metallic fragments embedded in the left thoracic wall, an oblique displaced fracture of the left fourth rib, marked hemopneumothorax with compression atelectasis, and pneumomediastinum, while excluding cranial or abdominal injury. At necropsy, approximately 100 mL of pleural blood was evacuated, and through-and-through pulmonary transcapsular lacerations were identified traversing the right and left cranial lung lobes. Multiple deformed metallic fragments were recovered adjacent to the fractured rib under strict forensic chain-of-custody protocols. Histopathology of pulmonary laceration margins confirmed acute hemorrhage, fibrin deposition, and early neutrophilic margination, establishing an acute antemortem vital reaction (survival interval < 1 h). Histological examination of the cutaneous entry and exit margins revealed mechanical tearing without thermal coagulation or soot residue, consistent with an intermediate-to-distant discharge. The anatomical convergence of lesions supported a right-to-left projectile trajectory, with the left axillary defect presenting features compatible with a shored exit wound. Death was attributed to fatal acute hemopneumothorax and bilateral pulmonary laceration secondary to perforating metallic projectile injury. This case demonstrates the indispensable diagnostic and prosecutorial value of integrating digital radiography, PMCT virtopsy, forensic necropsy, and histopathology in veterinary medicolegal investigations of non-accidental trauma.

records.title: Case Report: Presumptive subdural hemorrhage as a rare neurological manifestation of primary immune-mediated thrombocytopenia in a dog.
records.abstract: A 10-year-old female spayed mixed-breed dog was presented with a history of seizures and acute progressive intracranial signs. The neurological examination was consistent with multifocal brain disease. Clinical examination revealed ecchymoses, petechiae, and bilateral retinal hemorrhage. Clinicopathological evaluation identified severe thrombocytopenia [a platelet count of 9 × 10 3 /μL without clumps on manual smear evaluation] with an increased mean platelet volume. Coagulation testing (activated partial thromboplastin time and prothrombin time) and fibrinolysis markers (D-dimers, quantitative fibrinogen), infectious disease screening, and thoracic and abdominal imaging were within normal limits, establishing a diagnosis of primary immune-mediated thrombocytopenia (ITP). Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the brain showed minimally expanded, bilateral crescent-shaped, extra-axial fluid accumulations overlying both cerebral hemispheres. Based on T1-weighted and T2-weighted hyperintensities and peripheral susceptibility artifact on T2*-weighted gradient-recalled echo (GRE) imaging, a late subacute subdural intracranial hemorrhage was diagnosed. Despite initial uneventful anesthesia and recovery, the dog experienced acute neurological deterioration and suffered cardiopulmonary arrest, suspected due to ongoing hemorrhage or brain herniation. This report describes a rare neurological manifestation of primary ITP in a dog. While canine ITP generally carries a favorable prognosis, life-threatening secondary intracranial hemorrhage can occur. Primary ITP should be considered as a differential diagnosis for an acute, progressive neurological presentation until a normal platelet count is confirmed.

records.title: Primary Erythrophagocytic Low-Grade Splenic T-Cell Lymphoma in a Cat: Clinical Case and Literature Review.
records.journal: Animals : an open access journal from MDPI
records.abstract: Lymphoma is a common hematopoietic neoplasm in cats; yet hepatosplenic forms remain rare. This report describes a unique case of low-grade erythrophagocytic splenic T-cell lymphoma with suspected peripheral blood involvement in a six-year-old neutered male domestic shorthair cat. This confirmed a neoplastic T-cell population despite the mature morphology of the lymphocytes. Treatment with chlorambucil and prednisolone resulted in progressive resolution of the anemia. The cat remains alive 13 months after splenectomy. This case highlights the diagnostic challenges of low-grade lymphomas, in which reactive features can mask neoplasia, and underscores the critical role of PARR analysis in differentiating monoclonal T-cell proliferation from complex reactive processes in feline splenic disorders.

records.title: A novel 3D-printed patient-specific limb-sparing radial endoprosthesis for treatment of primary osteosarcoma in a Great Dane.
records.abstract: To describe a novel titanium three-dimensional-printed patient-specific radial endoprosthesis (3D-PSE) for the successful treatment of a primary osteosarcoma in a 7-year-old female Great Dane. Computed tomography (CT) revealed an osteolytic lesion involving the distal metaphysis and diaphysis of the radius which was highly suspicious for an osteosarcoma (OSA). Thoracic CT showed no metastases. CT data was used to create a virtual 3D-model of the affected limb within computer-aided design software which was used for virtual osteotomy planning and the design of the 3D-PSE. During surgery 3D-printed patient-specific guides were used to execute osteotomies. The 3D-PSE comprised plate sections for attachment to the proximal radius and metacarpals 3, 4 and 5, and an integrated cage for bone graft to replace the radial defect. records.title: Radiation therapy for persistent or progressive mediastinal lymphoma after chemotherapy in FeLV-positive cats: a retrospective case series of four cats.
records.abstract: Mediastinal lymphoma in feline leukaemia virus (FeLV)-positive cats is associated with a poor prognosis, and therapeutic options may be limited when adequate disease control is not achieved with chemotherapy. The efficacy of radiation therapy in this setting has not been established. Medical records were retrospectively reviewed for FeLV-positive cats diagnosed with mediastinal lymphoma between November 2018 and December 2024 that had persistent or progressive mediastinal disease after chemotherapy and were subsequently treated with radiation therapy. Treatment response was assessed by computed tomography using the Response Evaluation Criteria in Solid Tumours (RECIST). Three of four cats (75%) responded to radiation therapy (two complete responses, one partial response). Respiratory signs improved rapidly in three cats (median 5 days). Local disease control was achieved in most cases; however, three cats developed progression at other sites. Survival times were 45, 150 and 352 days in cats that died, and one cat remained alive for >626 days at the time of last follow-up. No severe radiation-related adverse effects were documented during the available follow-up, although systematic evaluation of late radiation toxicity was not possible. Radiation therapy may provide local control and rapid palliation of respiratory signs in FeLV-positive cats with persistent or progressive mediastinal lymphoma after chemotherapy. Further studies with larger cohorts are warranted.

records.title: Case report: long-term clinical remission of food-responsive enteropathy in a dog fed a yellow mealworm-based diet.
records.abstract: Food-responsive enteropathy (FRE) is the most common form of canine chronic inflammatory enteropathy. Novel protein diets constitute first-line therapy, and many dogs have already been exposed to "novel" meat alternatives. Edible insects are a novel, highly digestible, and sustainable protein source. In the present study, a five-year-old male York-shire Terrier with chronic FRE and gallbladder sludge was transitioned to a diet with a 35% inclusion level of  Tenebrio molitor  larvae meal. Clinical indices improved from "severe" (CIBDAI = 9 and CCECAI = 11) to "clinically insignificant" (CIBDAI = 0 and CCECAI = 2) within 3 weeks and remained stable for 24 months. Body weight normalized (from 5.4 to 4.0 kg), coat quality improved, and the ultrasound examination revealed that gallbladder sludge was eliminated. A brief interruption of the insect-based diet coincided with the recurrence of sludge and gastrointestinal signs, both of which resolved after the reintroduction of  T. molitor  larvae meal. Hematological and serum biochemical parameters remained within the reference ranges. The mealworm-based diet led to long-term remission of FRE and elimination of gallbladder sludge without adverse effects. Insect protein is a viable hypoallergenic option for canine elimination diets and may convey additional gut and hepatobiliary benefits.

records.title: Fibrostenotic intestinal stenosis associated with chronic enteropathy in two cats: case report.
records.abstract: Two cats presented with acute progressive vomiting. One cat (Case 1) received prednisolone for suspected chronic inflammatory enteropathy for 14 months. The cat showed hypoalbuminemia, hypocobalaminemia, small intestinal thickening, and focal jejunal stricture with severe proximal dilation on ultrasonography. The cat recovered uneventfully and remained restenosis-free during prednisolone treatment for 12 months after surgery. This suggests that the extent of the lesion and the surgical resection strategy could be relevant factors for management and prognosis.
